nodes.statement: (Period-2 stable oscillation and fixed point of two-step update F^2_eta.) Consider GD on a function f in domain Omega. Denote the update rule of GD as F_eta(x) for xinOmega with learning rate eta. A period-2 stable oscillation is exists~xinOmega such that F_eta(F_eta(x))=x and x is not a minima of f. Equivalently speaking, exists~xinOmega is a fixed point of the two-step update F^2_eta(cdot)triangleq F_eta(F_eta(cdot)).
nodes.raw_latex: (Period-2 stable oscillation and fixed point of two-step update $F^2_\eta$.) Consider GD on a function $f$ in domain $\Omega$. Denote the update rule of GD as $F_\eta(x)$ for $x\in\Omega$ with learning rate $\eta$. A \textbf{period-2 stable oscillation} is $\exists~x\in\Omega$ such that $F_\eta(F_\eta(x))=x$ and $x$ is not a minima of $f$. Equivalently speaking, $\exists~x\in\Omega$ is a \textbf{fixed point} of the two-step update $F^2_\eta(\cdot)\triangleq F_\eta(F_\eta(\cdot))$.

Denote the update rule of GD as F_eta(x) for xinOmega with learning rate eta. A period-2 stable oscillation is exists~xinOmega such that F_eta(F_eta(x))=x and x is not a minima of f. Equivalently speaking, exists~xinOmega is a fixed point of the two-step update F^2_eta(cdot)triangleq F_eta(F_eta(cdot)).

Consider any 1-D differentiable function $f(x)$ around a local minima $\Bar{x}$, satisfying (i) $f^{(3)}(\Bar{x})\neq 0$, and (ii) $3[f\T{3}]^2-f'' f\T{4}>0$ at $\Bar{x}$. \[
\frac{2}{f''(\Bar{x})}<\eta<\frac{2}{f''(\Bar{x})-\epsilon\cdot f^{(3)}(\Bar{x})}.
\]

\label{thm:1dlocal}

Consider any 1-D differentiable function $f(x)$ around a local minima $\Bar{x}$, satisfying that the lowest order non-zero derivative (except the $f''$) at $\Bar{x}$ is $f\T{k}(\Bar{x})$ with $k\ge 4$. Then, there exists $\epsilon$ with sufficiently small $|\epsilon|$ such that: for any point $x_0$ between $\Bar{x}$ and $\Bar{x}-\epsilon$, and
\begin{enumerate}
    \item if $k$ is odd and $\epsilon\cdot f\T{k}(\Bar{x})>0, f\T{k+1}(\Bar{x})<0$, 
    
    then there exists $\eta\in(\frac{2}{f''}, \frac{2}{f''-f\T{k}\epsilon^{k-2}})$,
    \item if $k$ is even and $f\T{k}(\Bar{x})<0$, then there exists $\eta\in(\frac{2}{f''}, \frac{2}{f''+f\T{k}\epsilon^{k-2}})$,
\end{enumerate}
such that: the update rule $F_\eta$ of GD satisfies $F_\eta(F_\eta(x_0))=x_0$.

Since k is odd and epsiloncdot fTk(Barx)>0, fTk+1(Barx)<0, the above two estimations of nicefracx_2-x_0eta have one positive and one negative exactly. First, we show the existence and uniqueness of such an orbit when Kin(1,1.5] via solving a high-order equation, some roots of which can be eliminated. Then, we conduct an analysis of global convergence by defining a special interval I. GD starting from any point following our assumption will enter I in some steps, and any point in I will back to this interval after two steps of iteration. Finally, any point in I will converge to the orbit (Barx_0, Barx_1). Before diving into the proof, we briefly show it always holds x>0 under our assumption. If x_t-1>0 and x_tle 0, the GD rule reveals eta(mu-x_t-1^2)le -1 which implies x_t-1^2 ge mu+frac1eta. However, the maximum of x+eta(mu-x^2)x on xin(0, sqrtmu+frac1eta) is achieved when x^2=frac13(mu+frac1eta) so the maximum value is sqrtfrac13(mu+frac1eta)(frac23+frac23etamu)le 1.4sqrtfrac13(mu+frac1eta)<sqrtmu+frac1eta. In this process, denote a series of all points with xy>mu as P=\(x_i,y_i)|x_i y_i>mu\. Then |x-y| reddecays to 0 in P, for any 1<K<1.5.

Meanwhile, we have x_t+1y_t+1 &=x_t y_t+etaleft(mu-x_t y_tright)left(x_t^2+y_t^2right)+eta^2left(mu-x_t y_tright)^2 x_t y_t nonumber \\ &= x_t y_tleft(1+etaleft(mu-x_t y_tright)right)^2 + etaleft(mu-x_t y_tright)left(x_t-y_tright)^2 Note that the second term in Eq() vanishes when x and y are balanced. Incorporating this inequality into Eq(, ) and assuming y_t-x_t>0, it holds y_t+2-x_t+2< left(y_t - x_tright) left(1-etaleft(mu-x_t y_tright)right) left(1-etaleft(mu-x_t y_tleft(1+etaleft(mu-x_t y_tright)right)^2right)right). To show that |x-y| is decaying as in the theorem, we are to show item y_t+2-x_t+2<y_t-x_t item y_t+2-x_t+2>-(y_t-x_t) Note that, although x_t y_t>mu, it is not sure to have x_t+2 y_t+2>mu. However, for any 0<x_i y_i<mu and K<2, we have frac|x_i+1-y_i+1||x_i-y_i|=left| 1-etaleft(mu-x_i y_iright)right| <1, which is saying |x-y| decays until it reaches xy>mu. It suffices to show eta (mu-b)+2(1+eta(mu-b))=2+3eta(mu-b)>0. Part II. To show y_t+2-x_t+2>-(y_t-x_t) Since x_t y_t>mu, we have 1-eta(mu-x_t y_t)>1. Combining with 1-eta(mu-x_t y_t)<2, it holds fracy_t+1-x_t+1y_t-x_t=1-eta(mu-x_t y_t)in(1,2). So the remaining is to have fracy_t+2-x_t+2y_t+1-x_t+1>-0.5. Actually it is 1-eta(mu-x_t+1y_t+1)ge 1-etamu=red1-K. red Therefore, we have fracy_t+2-x_t+2y_t-x_t> -1 +(3-2K), as required. red Part III. To show y_t-x_t converges to 0 From Exp (, , , ), we have for points in P, |y-x| is a monotone strictly decreasing sequence lower bounded by 0. Hence it is convergent. Actually it converges to 0. If not, assuming it converges to epsilon>0, the next point will have the difference as tildeepsilon<epsilon as well as all following points. Hence, the contradiction gives the convergence to 0.

nodes.statement: The proof is divided into two stages, depending on whether w_y grows or not. The key is that the change of w_y follows (omitting all superscripts t) fracDelta w_yw_y propto -vw_x+frac1pifracfracw_yw_x1+(fracw_yw_x)^2, ~~~~ w_y^(t+1) = left| w_y + Delta w_y right|. where the second term in nicefracDelta w_yw_y is bounded in [0, frac12pi]. In stage 1 where v w_x is relatively small, we show the growth ratio of w_y is smaller than those of w_x and vw_x, resulting in an upper bound of number of iterations for vw_x to reach frac12pi, so max(w_y) is bounded too. Although the initialization is balanced as vT0=normwT0 for simplicity of proof, v-w_x is also bounded at the end of stage 1. From the beginning of stage 2, thanks to the relatively narrow range of K, we are able to compute the bounds of three variables (including v-w_x, vw_x and w_y) and they turn out to fall into a basin in the parameter space after four iterations. In this basin, w_y decays exponentially with a linear rate of 0.97 at most.

For simplicity, we will omit all superscripts of time t unless clarification is necessary. From (), if the target is to show w_y decaying with a linear rate, it suffices to bound the factor term in () (by a considerable margin) as -2< Kleft(-v^2+fracv w_ypi normw^2right) <0. The technical part is the second inequality of (). If v, w_x>0, it is equivalent to v w_x>fracw_x w_ypi normw^2=fracw_x w_ypi (w_x^2+w_y^2), where the RHS is smaller than or equal to frac12pi. nodes.statement: For a matrix factorization problem, assume XY=C. Consider SVD of both matrices as X = sum_i=1^min\m,p\ sigma_x,i u_x,i v_x,i^top and Y = sum_i=1^min\p,q\ sigma_y,i u_y,i v_y,i^top, where both groups of sigma_cdot,i's are in descending order and both top singular values sigma_x,1 and sigma_y,1 are unique. Also assume v_x,1^top u_y,1neq 0. Then the leading eigenvector of the loss Hessian is Delta=vec(C_1 u_x,1u_y,1^top, C_2 v_x,1v_y,1^top) with C_1=fracsigma_y,1sqrtsigma_x,1^2+sigma_y,1^2, C_2=fracsigma_x,1sqrtsigma_x,1^2+sigma_y,1^2. Denote f_Delta as the 1D function at the cross section of the loss landscape and the line following the direction of Delta passing vec(DeltaX, DeltaY). Then, at the minima of f_Delta, it satisfies 3[f_Delta^(3)]^2 - f_Delta^(2)f_Delta^(4)>0.

nodes.statement: To obtain the direction of the leading Hessian eigenvector at parameters (X, Y), consider a small deviation of the parameters as (X+Delta X,Y+Delta Y). With XY=C, evaluate the loss function as L(X+Delta X,Y+Delta Y) &= frac12normDeltaXY + XDeltaY+DeltaXDeltaY_F^2. Expand these terms and split them by orders of DeltaX,DeltaY as follows: Theta(normDeltaX^2+normDeltaY^2):& ~~~~~frac12normDeltaXY + XDeltaY_F^2, \\ Theta(normDeltaX^3+normDeltaY^3):& ~~~~~langle DeltaXY + XDeltaY, DeltaXDeltaY rangle, \\ Theta(normDeltaX^4+normDeltaY^4):& ~~~~~frac12normDeltaXDeltaY_F^2. From the second-order terms, the leading eigenvector of nabla^2 L is the solution of vec(DeltaX, DeltaY) = mathoparg\,max_normDeltaX_F^2+normDeltaY_F^2 = 1normDeltaXY + XDeltaY_F^2. Since both the top singular values of X,Y are unique, the solution shall have both DeltaX, DeltaY of rank 1. Actually the solution is (here for simplicity we eliminate the sign of both) DeltaX = fracsigma_y,1sqrtsigma_x,1^2+sigma_y,1^2 u_x,1u_y,1^top, ~~~~DeltaY=fracsigma_x,1sqrtsigma_x,1^2+sigma_y,1^2 v_x,1v_y,1^top. Equipped with the top eigenvector of Hessian, vec(DeltaX, DeltaY), we consider the 1-D function f_Delta generated by the cross-section of the loss landscape and the eigenvector, passing the minima (X,Y). Define the function as f_Delta(mu) = L(X+muDeltaX, Y+muDeltaY), ~~~~muinR. Then, around mu=0, we have f_Delta(mu) = frac12normDeltaXY + XDeltaY_F^2cdot mu^2 + langle DeltaXY + XDeltaY, DeltaXDeltaY rangle cdot mu^3 + frac12normDeltaXDeltaY_F^2 cdot mu^4. Therefore, the several order derivatives of f_Delta(mu) at mu=0 can be obtained from Taylor expansion as f^(2)_Delta (0) &= normDeltaXY + XDeltaY_F^2, \\ f^(3)_Delta (0) &= 6langle DeltaXY + XDeltaY, DeltaXDeltaY rangle, \\ f^(4)_Delta (0) &= 12normDeltaXDeltaY_F^2. Then we compute the condition of stable oscillation of 1-D function as big[3[f_Delta^(3)]^2 - f_Delta^(2)f_Delta^(4)big] (0) &= 108 langle DeltaXY + XDeltaY, DeltaXDeltaY rangle^2 - 12 normDeltaXY + XDeltaY_F^2 normDeltaXDeltaY_F^2 \\ &= 96 normDeltaXY + XDeltaY_F^2 normDeltaXDeltaY_F^2 >0, because all of DeltaXY, XDeltaY, DeltaXDeltaY are parallel to u_x,1 v_y,1^top and v_x,1^top u_y,1neq 0.

nodes.statement: Consider the quasi-symmetric matrix factorization with learning rate eta = frac1sigma_1^2+beta. Assume 0<betasigma_1^2< sqrt4.5-1approx 1.121. Consider a minimum (Y_0=alphaX_0, Z_0=nicefrac1alphaX_0), alpha>0. The initialization is around the minimum, as Y_1 = Y_0 +Delta Y_1, Z_1 = Z_0 + Delta Z_1, with the deviations satisfying u_1^top DeltaY_1 v_1 neq 0, u_1^top DeltaZ_1 v_1 neq 0 and normDeltaY_1, normDeltaZ_1le epsilon. The second largest singular value of X_0 needs to satisfy etacdotmaxleft\ (fracsigma_1^2alpha^2+sigma_2^2alpha^2, fracsigma_2^2alpha^2+sigma_1^2alpha^2) right\ le 2. Then GD would converge to a period-2 orbit gamma_eta approximately with error in O(epsilon), formally written as (Y_t, Z_t) rightarrow gamma_eta + (DeltaY, DeltaZ), ~~~~~~normDeltaY, normDeltaZ=O(epsilon), \\\ gamma_eta = bigg\left(Y_0 + left(rho_i-alpharight) sigma_1 u_1 v_1^top , Z_0 + left(rho_i-nicefrac1alpharight) sigma_1 u_1 v_1^topright)bigg\, ~~~~~~(i=1,2) where rho_1in (1,2),rho_2in(0,1) are the two solutions of solving rho in 1+beta sigma_1^2 = frac1rho^2 left(sqrtfrac1rho^2-frac34+frac12 right).
